title: Red-Eyed, Hairy-Legged Sea Spiders Found in the Salish Sea
summary:
Imagine swimming at night and feeling tiny hairy legs crawl up your body. That creepy picture is now a real thing — sort of. Scientists at the University of British Columbia just found two brand-new species of sea spider in the Salish Sea. It's the first time in almost 100 years that anyone has described a new sea spider here.

Sea spiders are not actually spiders. They are ancient cousins of spiders and scorpions, and they have lived in the ocean for about 500 million years. Some have as many as 12 legs. Some are tiny, less than a centimeter long. Others in Antarctica grow bigger than a pizza box!

One new species is called Callipallene pilosuspedes. That name means "hairy feet" in Latin. It has long, curved spines on its legs and bright red eyes. Its mouth is split into three lips and ringed with feelers — kind of like a tiny Sarlacc pit from Star Wars.

Sea spiders are strange in other ways too. They breathe through their skin. The males carry the eggs, gluing them to their own bodies until they hatch.

Why does this matter? Scientists say we can't protect ocean animals if we don't even know their names. Now these two have names.
why_it_matters: This shows that even in the ocean near big cities, there are still animals nobody has named yet — so the nature close to home may hold surprises your class has never heard about.

background_read: The Salish Sea (the cold ocean water between the Canadian city of Vancouver and the U.S. state of Washington) is full of life, from whales and orcas to tiny worms on the sea floor.
Scientists at the University of British Columbia (a big research university in Canada) study the animals that live in this sea.
There are more than a thousand known kinds of sea spiders, and they live in oceans all over the world, from shallow beaches to the deep, dark sea floor.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at the University of British Columbia who study life in the Salish Sea
WHAT: They described two brand-new sea spider species, including Callipallene pilosuspedes, the 'hairy feet' one with long spines and bright red eyes
WHERE: In the Salish Sea, the ocean off Canada's west coast
WHY: It is the first new sea spider described there in almost 100 years, and scientists say you cannot protect ocean animals if you do not even know their names

perspectives.description: They say naming a new species is the first step to protecting it, and finding two in one place shows the sea is still full of hidden life.
People who dislike bugs might not enjoy the idea of hairy-legged creatures crawling on the sea floor, even though sea spiders do not hurt humans.
They point out that the Salish Sea faces pollution and warming water, and animals can disappear before scientists even give them a name.
